questions.scenarioContext: A 7-month-old infant needs a recumbent length. The clinic has an infant length board, and a second trained assistant is available.
questions.prompt: Which approach provides the most reliable measurement?

choices.A: Use the caregiver's reported birth length and adjust it for the infant's age.
choices.B: Use the length board with one assistant stabilizing the head and the other aligning the legs and footpiece.
choices.C: Place a tape along the infant's curved back while the caregiver holds the infant upright.
choices.D: Measure crown to heel while the infant sits with the knees comfortably bent.

questions.explanation: A length board and two-person positioning help align the infant from head to heel. Measuring along body curves or with flexed knees can give an inaccurate recumbent length.

questions.scenarioContext: An authorized assistant is preparing a patient's ordered intramuscular injection. The patient points to the intended arm and reports that the skin there is hot, red, and painful.
questions.prompt: What is the best next step?

choices.A: Inject into the reddest part because blood flow is increased.
choices.B: Change the ordered intramuscular route to subcutaneous without consultation.
choices.C: Pause and ask the clinician to evaluate the area and confirm a suitable site.
choices.D: Apply an ice pack and inject into the same area once it feels numb.

questions.explanation: A painful, inflamed area requires review before injection. The assistant should obtain a suitable site decision within the order and cannot independently change the route.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient is leaving with crutches after the provider has selected and ordered them. During the fitting check, the patient rests body weight on the axillary pads and reports hand tingling.
questions.prompt: Which response is appropriate?

choices.A: Stop the trial and have the trained clinician reassess fit and weight-bearing technique.
choices.B: Shorten both crutches without checking the ordered fitting procedure.
choices.C: Remove the handgrips so the patient must use the axillary pads.
choices.D: Tell the patient to bear more weight through the axillary pads.

questions.explanation: Weight through the axillary pads can place pressure on nerves and vessels. Tingling warrants stopping the trial and obtaining a proper fitting and technique review rather than encouraging more axillary loading.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient's completed safety screening includes the written response, "My partner hit me last night." The partner is not in the examination room, and clinic policy calls for prompt private clinician notification after a positive safety screen.
questions.prompt: What should the assistant do with this response?

choices.A: Complete the visit without alerting the clinician unless the patient repeats the report.
choices.B: Replace the response with a negative screen because no bruising is visible.
choices.C: Wait to ask the partner whether the account is accurate.
choices.D: Document the patient's words and promptly notify the clinician privately.

questions.explanation: A positive safety response should be preserved accurately and escalated under the supplied clinic procedure. Lack of visible injury does not negate the report, and questioning the partner can compromise safety.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient weighs 154 lb. The intake form requires kilograms, and its conversion instruction is kg = lb / 2.2, rounded to the nearest whole kilogram.
questions.prompt: Which weight should the assistant enter?

choices.A: 70 kg
choices.B: 68 kg
choices.C: 339 kg
choices.D: 75 kg

questions.explanation: 154 lb / 2.2 lb per kg = 70 kg. Multiplying by 2.2 converts in the opposite direction and does not provide the requested kilogram value.

questions.scenarioContext: A trained assistant is authorized to apply a prescribed transdermal patch. The product instructions require removal of the previous patch before a new one is applied. The prior patch is still on the patient's shoulder.
questions.prompt: Which action follows the order safely?

choices.A: Remove the prior patch as instructed before applying the new patch.
choices.B: Apply the new patch over the old patch to use the same site.
choices.C: Leave the old patch in place and apply the new patch beside it.
choices.D: Cut the new patch in half and leave the prior patch in place.

questions.explanation: The stated instructions prevent unintended exposure from overlapping patches. The assistant should follow removal, application, and disposal directions rather than altering the patch or stacking doses.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient cannot swallow an ordered tablet and asks the assistant to crush it. The assistant is trained and authorized for oral medication administration, but no information confirming that the tablet may be crushed is available.
questions.prompt: What should the assistant do?

choices.A: Crush the tablet because difficulty swallowing justifies changing any dosage form.
choices.B: Dissolve the tablet in a hot drink without checking its formulation.
choices.C: Pause administration and obtain pharmacist or prescriber guidance on an appropriate formulation.
choices.D: Give the patient a different person's liquid medication with a similar name.

questions.explanation: The tablet's suitability for crushing must be verified, and a formulation change may require a new order. Swallowing difficulty does not make every tablet safe to crush or dissolve.

questions.scenarioContext: A young infant has an order for capillary collection. The clinic's approved neonatal collection diagram specifies the medial or lateral plantar heel surface and prohibits the central and posterior heel. An age-appropriate depth-limited lancet is available.
questions.prompt: Which puncture site follows the supplied diagram?

choices.A: The curved posterior heel surface.
choices.B: An already bruised puncture site in the central heel.
choices.C: The lateral plantar surface within the approved heel area.
choices.D: The center of the plantar heel beneath the calcaneus.

questions.explanation: The lateral plantar area is one of the explicitly approved sites in the supplied neonatal procedure. The central and posterior heel are excluded, and an injured site should not be chosen.

questions.scenarioContext: An authorized, trained assistant has an order to give acetaminophen 480 mg orally. The verified liquid is labeled 160 mg per 5 mL. No rounding is needed.
questions.prompt: What volume is required for the ordered dose?

choices.A: 15 mL
choices.B: 30 mL
choices.C: 5 mL
choices.D: 10 mL

questions.explanation: 480 mg x 5 mL / 160 mg = 15 mL. A 5 mL volume provides only 160 mg, while 30 mL provides twice the ordered dose.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient waiting for a procedure has a seizure with generalized jerking. The assistant activates the emergency response, and staff begin clearing nearby equipment.
questions.prompt: Which additional action protects the patient?

choices.A: Give water during the jerking to prevent dehydration.
choices.B: Protect the head from injury and observe the duration without restraining the movements.
choices.C: Hold the arms and legs tightly against the examination table.
choices.D: Place a tongue depressor between the teeth to keep the mouth open.

questions.explanation: Protecting the patient from nearby hazards and noting seizure duration support emergency care. Restraint, objects in the mouth, and oral fluids can cause injury.

questions.category: Point of Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures
questions.scenarioContext: A patient is scheduled for distance visual-acuity screening. The clinic protocol says to test with the patient's usual distance correction and record whether correction was used. The patient normally wears distance glasses.
questions.prompt: How should the assistant perform and document the screening?

choices.A: Remove the glasses and document the test as corrected vision.
choices.B: Use the prior corrected acuity result in place of today's screening.
choices.C: Test through the distance glasses but document the result as uncorrected.
choices.D: Test with the distance glasses and document that correction was worn.

questions.explanation: Using and documenting the usual distance correction follows the supplied screening procedure. Corrected and uncorrected findings are not interchangeable and should not be mislabeled.

questions.category: Point of Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures
questions.scenarioContext: A provider orders a clean-catch midstream urine specimen. The patient asks whether to begin urinating directly into the collection cup. The supplied instructions call for initial urine into the toilet, then midstream collection without touching the inside of the cup.
questions.prompt: Which response reinforces the correct technique?

choices.A: Collect the first drops directly into the cup before any urine enters the toilet.
choices.B: Begin in the toilet, then collect the midstream portion without touching the cup interior.
choices.C: Touch the cup interior to the skin so no urine spills.
choices.D: Fill the cup from the toilet bowl after voiding.

questions.explanation: The supplied clean-catch procedure uses a midstream portion while protecting the container interior from contamination. Collecting the initial drops or toilet-bowl urine does not follow that procedure.

questions.scenarioContext: For a standard 12-lead EKG, V4 is correctly placed in the fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line. The assistant now needs to place V6.
questions.prompt: Which position is correct for V6?

choices.A: Left anterior axillary line at the same horizontal level as V4.
choices.B: Right midaxillary line at the same horizontal level as V4.
choices.C: Left midaxillary line at whichever intercostal space lies directly below V4.
choices.D: Left midaxillary line at the same horizontal level as V4.

questions.explanation: V6 is positioned on the left midaxillary line, horizontally aligned with V4. The left anterior axillary location at that level corresponds to V5.

questions.scenarioContext: A venous additive tube has just filled. Its manufacturer instructs staff to mix by five gentle inversions and warns against vigorous shaking.
questions.prompt: Which technique follows the instruction?

choices.A: Open the tube and stir it with a collection needle.
choices.B: Turn the tube end over end gently five times.
choices.C: Leave the tube upright without mixing.
choices.D: Shake the tube rapidly until foam appears.

questions.explanation: Five gentle inversions follow the supplied mixing requirement without unnecessary mechanical damage. Vigorous shaking can contribute to hemolysis, while inadequate mixing can leave additive distribution uneven.

questions.scenarioContext: A used injection needle has a built-in safety shield. The assistant has completed the injection and is beside an approved sharps container.
questions.prompt: Which disposal action is appropriate?

choices.A: Place the exposed needle on the tray for later disposal.
choices.B: Recap the needle with both hands before carrying it to the container.
choices.C: Remove the needle by hand and place it in a regular wastebasket.
choices.D: Activate the safety feature as instructed and discard the device promptly into the sharps container.

questions.explanation: Prompt disposal with the device safety feature reduces exposure to a contaminated sharp. Routine two-handed recapping, manual removal, or leaving the sharp exposed creates avoidable injury risk.

questions.category: Point of Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures
questions.scenarioContext: A patient performing ordered spirometry stops blowing after 1 second, although the device indicates that expiration is incomplete. The written protocol requires an acceptable sustained effort and repeat coaching before a result is accepted.
questions.prompt: What should the assistant do?

choices.A: Explain and demonstrate the sustained exhalation again, then repeat according to protocol.
choices.B: Select the largest displayed number from the failed attempts as the final result.
choices.C: Accept the brief effort as the final result because some air was exhaled.
choices.D: Record the incomplete effort as acceptable if its first second looks smooth.

questions.explanation: A prematurely ended effort does not meet the supplied acceptance criterion. Coaching and an appropriate repeat are preferable to estimating missing data or accepting an unacceptable maneuver.

questions.category: Point of Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures
questions.scenarioContext: Before ordered skin allergy testing, the clinic protocol requires clinician review if an antihistamine was taken within the past 48 hours. The patient reports taking an antihistamine that morning and has no current symptoms.
questions.prompt: What should the assistant do before testing begins?

choices.A: Proceed with testing and omit the medication because the patient feels well.
choices.B: Increase the test allergen amount to compensate for the antihistamine.
choices.C: Tell the patient to stop every prescription for a week and return without clinician review.
choices.D: Document the medication and time taken and obtain the testing clinician's instructions.

questions.explanation: The reported medication use triggers the explicitly supplied pretest review rule. The assistant should obtain clinician instructions rather than independently changing medications or modifying the test.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient rates knee pain as 8 on a 0-10 scale, sits quietly, and smiles during conversation. The assistant sees no visible injury.
questions.prompt: How should the assistant document the pain?

choices.A: Lower the rating to 3 because the patient is smiling.
choices.B: Record the patient's rating and relevant reported features of the pain.
choices.C: Record severe tissue damage as the cause of the reported pain.
choices.D: Omit the rating until a visible cause is identified.

questions.explanation: Pain ratings reflect the patient's report and should be documented with location and other relevant details. Appearance alone does not justify changing the score or assigning a diagnosis.

questions.scenarioContext: A blood glucose meter is approved by its manufacturer for use on multiple patients. Its instructions require cleaning and disinfection after every patient using the specified compatible product.
questions.prompt: What should the assistant do before using it for the next patient?

choices.A: Place the meter in a clean bag without disinfecting it.
choices.B: Change the test strip without processing the meter.
choices.C: Complete the specified cleaning and disinfection process.
choices.D: Wipe only the display with a dry tissue.

questions.explanation: A shared meter can carry contamination even when a fresh strip is used. The manufacturer's complete between-patient processing instructions must be followed.

questions.scenarioContext: A regular EKG is recorded at 25 mm/s. The supplied reference states that each large box represents 0.2 seconds at this speed. Consecutive R waves are five large boxes apart.
questions.prompt: What ventricular rate does this interval represent?

choices.A: 75 beats/min
choices.B: 100 beats/min
choices.C: 150 beats/min
choices.D: 60 beats/min

questions.explanation: Five large boxes x 0.2 seconds per box = 1 second per beat. 60 seconds per minute / 1 second per beat = 60 beats/min; this calculation describes rate without selecting a diagnosis or treatment.

questions.prompt: Which instrument is designed to remove skin staples?

choices.A: A skin staple remover.
choices.B: A hemostat.
choices.C: A needle holder.
choices.D: Fine tissue forceps.

questions.explanation: A staple remover lifts and reshapes skin staples for removal. A needle holder is used to control a suturing needle and is not the designated staple-removal instrument.

questions.scenarioContext: A sealed sterile pack is found wet after storage beneath a leaking pipe. The wrapper is otherwise intact, and the pack is needed for a procedure.
questions.prompt: Which action is appropriate?

choices.A: Place a dry towel around the pack and use it immediately.
choices.B: Let the wrapper dry and return the pack to sterile stock.
choices.C: Use only instruments from the center of the wet pack.
choices.D: Remove the pack from sterile stock and obtain an uncompromised pack.

questions.explanation: Moisture can compromise a sterile barrier and allow contamination. Drying the outside does not establish that the contents remained sterile.

questions.scenarioContext: A comfortable adult is seated for a routine blood pressure measurement with crossed legs, an unsupported back, and the cuffed arm hanging beside the chair.
questions.prompt: Which setup best supports an accurate resting measurement?

choices.A: Keep the legs crossed and support the arm at heart level after the patient rests.
choices.B: Support the back and arm at heart level, with feet flat and legs uncrossed.
choices.C: Support the back and feet but leave the cuffed arm hanging freely at the side.
choices.D: Have the patient lean forward and hold the cuffed arm unsupported at chest height.

questions.explanation: Back support, uncrossed legs, flat feet, and an arm supported at heart level reduce positioning errors. Holding an arm up without support is not equivalent to resting it on a support.

questions.scenarioContext: During EKG preparation, a patient becomes dizzy and reports chest discomfort. The monitor displays a rate of 38 beats/min with a stable signal, and the assistant can feel a slow pulse.
questions.prompt: What should the assistant do next?

choices.A: Finish cleaning every cable before informing the clinician.
choices.B: Summon the clinician immediately and activate the clinic emergency response as indicated.
choices.C: Choose an antiarrhythmic medication based on the displayed rate.
choices.D: Assume electrical interference and leave the patient alone to obtain another machine.

questions.explanation: Symptoms with a confirmed slow pulse require prompt patient-focused escalation. Equipment tasks must not delay care, and selecting cardiac medication is beyond the assistant's role.

questions.category: Point of Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures
questions.scenarioContext: A test's collection instructions require a specific transport swab and medium. The assistant finds that the swab just collected from the throat is in a different, incompatible transport medium; no result has been produced.
questions.prompt: Which action is appropriate?

choices.A: Transfer the used swab into the correct medium and assume the sample is acceptable.
choices.B: Notify the clinician and arrange recollection with the required collection system.
choices.C: Send the incompatible system without documenting the medium problem.
choices.D: Hold the specimen until courier pickup and substitute the correct medium then.

questions.explanation: The specified collection system is part of the test's validated handling requirements. Relabeling or transferring after incompatible exposure does not establish acceptability.

questions.scenarioContext: A fasting laboratory order includes written instructions for an 8-hour fast and directs staff to contact the ordering clinician if the preparation was not followed. The patient reports eating breakfast 2 hours before arrival.
questions.prompt: Which action should the assistant take?

choices.A: Collect and document an 8-hour fast because the order requested it.
choices.B: Tell the patient to stop all medications and return after a 24-hour fast.
choices.C: Report the actual preparation and obtain instructions before proceeding under the fasting order.
choices.D: Perform a random test instead by changing the order independently.

questions.explanation: The stated order requires clarification when fasting preparation is not met. Accurate reporting allows the clinician to decide whether to collect, reschedule, or change the order; the assistant should not make that clinical change.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient arrives coughing, reports recent fever, and is waiting near other patients. The clinic respiratory-hygiene procedure directs staff to offer a mask if tolerated, separate symptomatic patients, and promptly notify clinical staff.
questions.prompt: Which action follows the procedure?

choices.A: Delay notifying clinical staff until the patient has completed all paperwork.
choices.B: Ask the patient to remove a tolerated mask when speaking to registration.
choices.C: Keep the patient in the crowded waiting area until the cough stops.
choices.D: Offer a mask, move the patient to the designated separate area, and alert clinical staff.

questions.explanation: The stated procedure combines source control, separation, and prompt clinical notification. Waiting for paperwork leaves other patients exposed and delays evaluation.

questions.scenarioContext: An assistant is opening an intact sterile tray wrapper on a clean, dry work surface. The first outer flap is folded across the far side of the tray, and the sterile contents must remain untouched.
questions.prompt: How should the assistant open the first flap?

choices.A: Open the far flap toward the body while reaching across the sterile contents.
choices.B: Grasp the inner surface of the far flap and pull it toward the body.
choices.C: Grasp the outside of the far flap and open it away from the body.
choices.D: Place an ungloved hand on the sterile contents to stabilize the wrapper.

questions.explanation: Opening the far flap away from the body avoids reaching over the exposed sterile contents. Handling the outer wrapper rather than its sterile interior helps preserve the field.

questions.scenarioContext: After venipuncture, a patient taking an anticoagulant still has oozing at the puncture site. The assistant is holding clean gauze over the site, and the patient is otherwise stable.
questions.prompt: Which action is appropriate?

choices.A: Ask the patient to bend the elbow tightly and leave without checking the site.
choices.B: Apply a bandage over the actively oozing site and send the patient away.
choices.C: Tell the patient to stop the anticoagulant for the next week.
choices.D: Maintain direct pressure, monitor for hemostasis, and notify the clinician if bleeding persists.

questions.explanation: Continued direct pressure and confirmation that bleeding has stopped are important before departure. The assistant should report persistent bleeding and must not independently stop prescribed anticoagulant therapy.

questions.scenarioContext: An authorized, trained assistant is preparing an ordered 0.75 mg intramuscular dose. The verified vial contains 1.5 mg/mL, and a syringe graduated in 0.1 mL increments is available. No rounding is needed.
questions.prompt: What volume corresponds to the order?

choices.B: 1 mL
choices.C: 0.5 mL
choices.D: 2 mL

questions.explanation: 0.75 mg / 1.5 mg per mL = 0.5 mL. The order and supplied concentration must be used with their units; a decimal-place error would give a tenfold underdose.

questions.category: Point of Care Testing and Laboratory Procedures
questions.scenarioContext: A courier is collecting a stool specimen for a test whose collection sheet requires an approved dry, clean container and no contact with urine or toilet water. The patient reports that the submitted sample fell into the toilet before transfer to the cup.
questions.prompt: What should the assistant do?

choices.A: Send the sample without noting the collection problem because the container is sealed.
choices.B: Accept the sample because moving it into a clean cup removes the contamination.
choices.C: Apply the rejection policy, notify the appropriate staff, and arrange a properly collected replacement.
choices.D: Accept the sample if no toilet water is visible in the cup.

questions.explanation: The reported collection violates the stated specimen requirements and can affect results. A clean outer cup does not undo prior contact with toilet water.

questions.scenarioContext: During previsit planning, a medical assistant sees a colorectal screening reminder in the electronic health record. The patient reports having a colonoscopy at an outside facility last year, but the report is absent. The provider will review screening needs at tomorrow's visit.
questions.prompt: Which action best prepares the record for the provider's review?

choices.A: Mark the screening complete using the patient's estimate of the procedure date.
choices.B: Keep the reminder active without recording the reported outside procedure.
choices.C: Document the patient's report and request the outside procedure report through the approved process.
choices.D: Enter a new screening due date using the usual interval for colonoscopy.

questions.explanation: Recording the patient-reported history and seeking the actual report gives the provider information needed to determine screening status. A reported procedure should not be treated as a verified result or used by the assistant to establish a new screening interval.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient confirms attending an ordered cardiology consultation two weeks ago. The referral tracker still shows an open referral, and the primary care record contains no consultation report. The patient's next primary care visit is in two days.
questions.prompt: What should the medical assistant do to move this referral toward closure?

choices.A: Request the consultation report, route it for provider review, and track any required follow-up.
choices.B: Close the referral after documenting that the patient attended the appointment.
choices.C: Ask the patient to summarize the recommendations and use that summary as the consultation report.
choices.D: Send a duplicate cardiology referral so a new consultation can generate another report.

questions.explanation: Attendance alone does not establish that the referring team received and acted on the specialist's recommendations. Obtaining the report, routing it for clinical review, and tracking the resulting follow-up supports continuity without asking the assistant to interpret the findings.

questions.scenarioContext: A provider has ordered a home blood pressure monitor and approved a device-specific teaching checklist. After the assistant demonstrates the checklist steps, the patient says, "I understand." The assistant needs to evaluate whether the instruction was effective.
questions.prompt: Which finding provides the best evidence that the patient can perform the task?

choices.A: The patient states that the written instructions look familiar.
choices.B: The patient agrees to read the monitor booklet before using it.
choices.C: The patient identifies the monitor's brand and model correctly.
choices.D: The patient performs the measurement steps correctly using the checklist.

questions.explanation: A return demonstration directly shows whether the patient can carry out the taught procedure. Agreement or recognition of the device does not demonstrate correct technique; the assistant should address any observed errors and recheck performance.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient has missed two ordered physical therapy appointments because a wheelchair-accessible ride is unavailable. The patient wants to attend and agrees to assistance. A clinic resource directory lists an accessible ride program, but reservation requirements have not been confirmed.
questions.prompt: Which coordination action best addresses the stated barrier?

choices.A: Move therapy to a later month and close the transportation task until the patient calls again.
choices.B: Contact the ride program with the patient to confirm access and booking needs, then verify the ride arrangement.
choices.C: Reschedule the same appointment time and remind the patient to arrange transportation.
choices.D: Give the patient a list of general taxi companies and mark the barrier resolved.

questions.explanation: The barrier is access to a suitable ride, so coordination must establish whether the resource can meet the patient's mobility and scheduling needs. A specific booking plan and follow-up are more useful than another reminder or an unverified list of transportation options.

questions.scenarioContext: On October 6, an assistant reviews a provider's documented recommendation that a patient complete a screening mammogram during November. The patient agrees with that plan. The clinic's reminder system currently shows the task as due in October.
questions.prompt: How should the assistant maintain the preventive-care tracking task?

choices.A: Close the task because the provider has already discussed screening with the patient.
choices.B: Align the tracking task with the documented November recommendation and retain follow-up until completion is verified.
choices.C: Keep the October due date because the reminder system should override the visit note.
choices.D: Change the recommendation to December to give the patient an additional month to schedule.

questions.explanation: The tracking task should reflect the provider's documented plan and remain active until the screening status is resolved. Discussing a screening is not the same as completing it, and the assistant should not create a different clinical timeline.

questions.scenarioContext: During a post-discharge call, a patient reports that the hospital paperwork and a prescription bottle show different doses of the same medication. The patient asks which dose to take. Clinic policy directs medication discrepancies to the nurse or provider for prompt clarification.
questions.prompt: Which response stays within the assistant's role?

choices.A: Use the dose on the bottle because it was dispensed by a pharmacy.
choices.B: Use the discharge dose because hospital instructions are more recent.
choices.C: Recommend a dose between the two until the follow-up appointment.
choices.D: Document both instructions and arrange prompt clarification by the nurse or provider under clinic policy.

questions.explanation: The discrepancy needs clinical clarification, and both sources should be available to the licensed team member resolving it. Selecting either dose based only on its source or apparent date would make an unauthorized medication decision.

questions.scenarioContext: A provider's written nutrition plan asks a patient to replace one sugar-sweetened drink each day with water. The patient says, "I can do that, but my workplace has only a soda vending machine." The assistant is reinforcing this established goal.
questions.prompt: Which action best supports the patient's self-management?

choices.A: Help the patient plan how to bring water to work and agree on a way to track the daily substitution.
choices.B: Provide a beverage handout and defer planning for water access until the next follow-up visit.
choices.C: Ask the patient to repeat the goal at each visit without discussing workplace arrangements.
choices.D: Suggest waiting to begin the goal until the workplace installs a drinking fountain.

questions.explanation: A practical plan for obtaining water addresses the patient's stated obstacle while preserving the provider's goal. Tracking the substitution supports follow-up; prescribing a different diet or simply repeating the instruction does not address the implementation problem.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient reports running out of food before the end of each month and being unable to obtain the foods in a dietitian's existing plan. The patient would like help. The clinic has a resource navigator who can assess food-program eligibility and local food availability.
questions.prompt: Which action best connects the patient with useful support?

choices.A: Provide a low-cost grocery list and document the food-access issue as resolved.
choices.B: Suggest buying foods in bulk and defer resource assistance until the next visit.
choices.C: Connect the patient with the resource navigator for food assistance and track whether contact occurs.
choices.D: Document that the patient prefers other foods and leave the plan unchanged without follow-up.

questions.explanation: Food insecurity is a resource barrier that needs a specific assistance connection and follow-up. The assistant can facilitate that connection without revising the dietitian's clinical plan or assuming the patient is unwilling to follow it.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient has not completed a provider-recommended screening mammogram. During outreach, the patient says the scheduling call was confusing and they remain unsure how to proceed. The patient has not said that they refuse the screening.
questions.prompt: Which entry and follow-up best support accurate care-gap tracking?

choices.A: Document the scheduling difficulty, offer scheduling assistance, and retain the task for follow-up.
choices.B: Document screening refusal and close the task because the test remains incomplete.
choices.C: Mark the screening complete because outreach has now been performed.
choices.D: Remove the recommendation because the patient has not scheduled it independently.

questions.explanation: The record should reflect the barrier the patient actually describes. Scheduling assistance and continued tracking address that barrier; an incomplete screening should not be relabeled as refusal or completion merely to close the task.

questions.scenarioContext: The provider orders home health nursing after a patient's discharge. The assistant securely sends the order to an agency. The agency replies that it has no available staff and has not accepted the referral. Clinic policy requires notifying the ordering team and arranging an accepting agency through that team.
questions.prompt: What should the assistant do next?

choices.A: Record the fax transmission as a completed home health referral.
choices.B: Tell the patient to start the home nursing visits when an agency becomes available.
choices.C: Notify the ordering team of the declined referral and help locate an accepting agency under the ordered plan.
choices.D: Cancel home health nursing and ask the family to provide the ordered services.

questions.explanation: Successful transmission does not establish that a service will be provided. A declined referral must return to the ordering team so another agency can be coordinated and the service start tracked without the assistant changing the care plan.

questions.scenarioContext: During a virtual visit, an assistant reinforces the provider's written home-care plan. The patient can access the handout but loses track when all six instructions are reviewed together. The connection is clear, and the patient wants to continue.
questions.prompt: Which teaching adjustment best addresses the observed difficulty?

choices.A: Read all six instructions more quickly so the patient hears them as a single message.
choices.B: Review a small group of instructions, ask the patient to explain that part in their own words, and then continue.
choices.C: Send a longer handout and end the teaching without checking understanding.
choices.D: Ask whether the patient understands after repeating the full list in the same way.

questions.explanation: Breaking information into manageable segments and checking understanding after each segment allows errors to be identified and corrected before moving on. Repeating the same long presentation or asking only for a yes-or-no response does not establish understanding.

questions.scenarioContext: Before a child's visit, the assistant reviews an outside immunization record. The electronic health record lists two doses of the same vaccine on the same date, but the outside record shows only one administration. The provider has asked the assistant to prepare a verified immunization history before reviewing today's needs.
questions.prompt: How should the assistant handle the discrepancy?

choices.A: Count both electronic entries as separate doses when preparing the history.
choices.B: Delete one entry immediately because same-day entries must be duplicates.
choices.C: Use the discrepancy to choose which vaccine dose the child should receive today.
choices.D: Flag the conflicting entries, verify the source details, and route the discrepancy through the clinic's correction process.

questions.explanation: Conflicting documentation should be verified and corrected through the approved process before it is treated as an accurate history. The assistant should neither count uncertain entries as distinct administrations nor independently decide the child's vaccine needs.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient who cares for a spouse with memory impairment says they cannot attend their own follow-up visits because the spouse cannot be left alone. The patient requests information about supervised daytime support. The clinic directory includes an adult day services program and a respite resource coordinator.
questions.prompt: Which referral best matches this barrier?

choices.A: A caregiver education group to teach the patient more about memory impairment.
choices.B: A meal delivery program to reduce the time the patient spends preparing food.
choices.C: The respite coordinator to explore appropriate daytime supervision and availability before the next visit.
choices.D: A telephone check-in service to call the spouse while the patient attends appointments.

questions.explanation: The patient needs a workable supervision resource to make attendance possible. A respite coordinator can help identify suitable daytime options and availability; a telephone check-in does not provide the supervision described as necessary.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient is scheduled for a primary care follow-up after an emergency department visit. A discharge summary identifies a pending urine culture, but no result is in the clinic record. The clinic workflow assigns the follow-up nurse to track pending transition results and the provider to interpret them.
questions.prompt: Which handoff best supports continuity for this visit?

choices.A: File the discharge summary and omit the pending culture because it has no final result yet.
choices.B: Alert the follow-up nurse to the pending culture, record the result source and status, and track routing for provider review.
choices.C: Tell the patient that the culture was probably normal because no result has been received.
choices.D: Ask the laboratory for a preliminary finding and use it to recommend a medication change.

questions.explanation: A reliable transition handoff identifies unfinished testing and connects it to the team member responsible for tracking and clinical review. A missing result is not evidence of a normal result, and the assistant must not use laboratory findings to select treatment.

questions.scenarioContext: An assistant reinforces a provider-approved communicable-disease prevention handout with a parent. The handout includes washing hands before preparing food and after using the toilet. During teach-back, the parent describes washing only when the hands look dirty.
questions.prompt: Which action best completes this teaching encounter?

choices.A: Use a concrete daily example to review the missed handwashing times, then ask the parent to explain the plan again.
choices.B: Document that teaching was understood because the parent participated in teach-back.
choices.C: Repeat the handout word for word and finish without another understanding check.
choices.D: Offer an extra copy of the handout and defer checking the missed point until the next visit.

questions.explanation: Teach-back has revealed a specific misunderstanding, so the assistant should explain that point differently and check again. Participation in teach-back is not itself evidence of learning; the response must reflect the preventive actions in the established instructions.

questions.scenarioContext: A clinic requires a 30-minute appointment for a new pediatric patient. A qualified interpreter must attend the entire visit. The provider has openings from 9:00 to 9:15 a.m., 10:00 to 10:30 a.m., 10:30 to 11:00 a.m., and 11:00 to 11:30 a.m. The interpreter is available only from 10:00 to 10:30 a.m.
questions.prompt: Which appointment should the medical assistant schedule?
questions.explanation: The 10:00 to 10:30 a.m. opening provides the required 30 minutes with both the provider and interpreter available. The shorter opening cannot accommodate the visit, and the later openings do not match interpreter availability.

questions.scenarioContext: At check-in, a patient presents a new insurance card and says that coverage through a former employer ended last month. The practice-management system still lists the former plan as active. No eligibility check has been completed for today.
questions.prompt: Which action best establishes the information needed for billing this visit?

choices.A: Keep the former plan because the system labels it active.
choices.B: Use the new card as proof that all services today are covered.
choices.C: Enter both plans as active primary coverage for the visit.
choices.D: Verify the new plan for the service date and update the account with the confirmed information.

questions.explanation: The assistant should verify current eligibility for the date of service and update the account with confirmed plan information. A card or an old active flag does not establish current benefits. Any remaining discrepancy should be resolved through the office verification process.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly identifies the code sets used for diagnoses and for procedures or services on outpatient medical claims?

choices.A: ICD-10-CM for diagnoses; CPT/HCPCS for procedures or services.
choices.B: CPT/HCPCS for diagnoses; ICD-10-CM for procedures or services.
choices.C: ICD-10-PCS for diagnoses; CPT/HCPCS for procedures or services.
choices.D: ICD-10-CM for diagnoses; ICD-10-PCS for routine office procedures.

questions.explanation: ICD-10-CM describes diagnoses, and CPT/HCPCS identifies procedures, services, and applicable items or supplies. ICD-10-PCS is used for inpatient hospital procedure coding rather than routine physician-office procedure claims. Selection of a code must be supported by the encounter documentation.

questions.scenarioContext: An assistant finds an outside consultation report indexed in the wrong electronic chart. The two patients have the same first and last names but different dates of birth and medical record numbers. Office policy requires staff to report indexing errors to the records coordinator, who uses a correction workflow that preserves the audit trail.
questions.prompt: What should the assistant do?

choices.A: Change the report date of birth to match the chart where it appears.
choices.B: Upload a second copy into the other chart and leave the first copy in place.
choices.C: Confirm the report identifiers and notify the records coordinator for correction through the designated workflow.
choices.D: Delete the report and ask the specialist to create a replacement report.

questions.explanation: The identifiers establish that the report was indexed to the wrong patient, and the stated policy specifies how to correct it. The assistant should initiate that process without altering the clinical report. Simply adding another copy leaves inaccurate information in the original chart.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately describes prior authorization from a health insurance plan?

choices.A: It is an advance approval decision that does not guarantee payment for the service.
choices.B: It confirms that the patient has already met the annual deductible.
choices.C: It replaces any separate referral requirement under the plan.
choices.D: It fixes the final amount the patient will owe for the service.

questions.explanation: Prior authorization is an advance approval decision, not a guarantee that the plan will pay a claim. Eligibility, benefits, and other applicable claim requirements still matter. It does not by itself establish deductible status, replace a separate referral requirement, or determine the final patient balance.

questions.scenarioContext: An established patient calls for a routine appointment but reports new dizziness that began this morning. The clinic telephone protocol directs scheduling staff to connect callers reporting new dizziness to the clinical nurse immediately. The nurse is available to take the call.
questions.prompt: Which action follows the stated workflow?

choices.A: Book the next routine opening and add dizziness to the appointment note.
choices.B: Connect the caller to the clinical nurse now and document the handoff.
choices.C: Ask the caller to try a home remedy before choosing an appointment.
choices.D: Decide whether the dizziness is severe enough to require a same-day visit.

questions.explanation: The supplied protocol calls for an immediate clinical handoff, so the assistant should connect the caller to the available nurse and document that action. Choosing the urgency independently would exceed the scheduling role. Routine booking alone would bypass the required clinical review.

questions.scenarioContext: An in-network covered service has a $240 allowed amount. The plan applies the patient's remaining $60 deductible first, then charges 20% coinsurance on the rest. There is no copayment, no other charge, and no out-of-pocket maximum adjustment. The patient already paid $30 toward this service. For this exercise, these amounts are final.
questions.prompt: What additional amount remains for the patient to pay?
questions.explanation: After the $60 deductible, $180 remains; 20% of $180 is $36. Total patient responsibility is $60 + $36 = $96. Subtracting the $30 already paid leaves $66 due; $96 would ignore the posted payment.

questions.scenarioContext: A clinic has 14 usable packs of examination-table paper and no outstanding order. It uses two packs per clinic day. An order placed now will arrive after five clinic days of use, before the next clinic day begins. Office policy sets the reorder point at expected use during delivery time plus four safety-stock packs.
questions.prompt: Which inventory action follows the policy?

choices.A: Wait three clinic days because the current stock covers a full week.
choices.B: Wait until four packs remain because those packs represent the reorder point.
choices.C: Place an order now because the current stock equals the 14-pack reorder point.
choices.D: Place an order after five clinic days because deliveries take five days.

questions.explanation: Expected use during delivery is 2 packs/day x 5 days = 10 packs. Adding the four-pack safety stock gives a reorder point of 14 packs, so an order is due now. Waiting until only the safety stock remains would fail to account for supplies needed during delivery.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient has a nonurgent specialist visit scheduled next week. The plan requires both a primary care referral and a separate authorization for this visit. The signed referral is in the chart, but the payer portal shows no authorization request. Office policy assigns authorization submission and tracking to the referral coordinator.
questions.prompt: Which action should the medical assistant take?

choices.A: Mark the authorization approved because the primary care referral is signed.
choices.B: Send the referral and required documentation to the coordinator and track the authorization status before the visit.
choices.C: Change the referral diagnosis to one that is more likely to receive approval.
choices.D: Tell the patient that the missing authorization means the plan has denied the visit.

questions.explanation: The stem specifies two separate requirements, and only the referral has been completed. Routing the documentation to the designated coordinator and tracking the request addresses the missing authorization. A request that has not been submitted is not a denial, and the assistant must not change a diagnosis to obtain payment.

questions.scenarioContext: A claim denial states that the submitted member identification number does not match the payer's enrollment record. The current insurance card and the payer's verified record agree, but the submitted claim omitted one digit. The documented services and diagnosis are correct. The payer provides a corrected-claim process for this error.
questions.prompt: Which action addresses the reason for denial?

choices.A: Correct the member identification number and follow the payer's corrected-claim process.
choices.B: Resubmit the same claim unchanged because the services were documented.
choices.C: Change the diagnosis code before submitting a new claim.
choices.D: Move the entire charge to patient responsibility without correcting the claim.

questions.explanation: The verified mismatch identifies a demographic claim error, so the assistant should correct that field and use the payer's stated process. Resubmitting unchanged would preserve the cause of denial. Accurate service documentation does not compensate for an incorrect member identifier.

questions.scenarioContext: An older adult misses an ordered follow-up visit. The scheduling policy requires staff to record the missed visit, contact the patient through the approved reminder system to offer rescheduling, and send a task to the clinical team when no replacement appointment is arranged. A call reaches voicemail, and no new appointment is scheduled.
questions.prompt: Which documentation and follow-up are appropriate?

choices.A: Record that the follow-up is complete because a reminder was sent.
choices.B: Remove the visit from the schedule and wait for the patient to call.
choices.C: Record that the patient declined care because the call was unanswered.
choices.D: Record the missed visit and contact attempt, then route the unresolved follow-up task to the clinical team.

questions.explanation: The record should accurately show both the missed visit and the contact attempt, with escalation as the stated policy requires. Reaching voicemail does not establish refusal or complete the follow-up. The clinical team can then review the unresolved follow-up need within its role.

questions.scenarioContext: An uninsured patient asks about help paying for a scheduled visit. The practice has a financial assistance program with a standard application. Only the financial counselor may determine eligibility or approve payment arrangements, and the counselor is available.
questions.prompt: Which response is within the medical assistant's administrative role?

choices.A: Promise a fee waiver based on the patient's description of income.
choices.B: Provide the program application and connect the patient with the financial counselor.
choices.C: Tell the patient to enroll in the program without completing an application.
choices.D: Assign a payment plan and ask the counselor to approve it afterward.

questions.explanation: The assistant can provide the established application and direct the patient to the staff member authorized to review eligibility and payment arrangements. This gives access to the office process without making an unsupported financial promise. Approval remains with the counselor under the stated policy.

questions.scenarioContext: A technician services an examination-room scale and leaves a report documenting satisfactory operation. The report lists the service date, equipment serial number, work performed, technician, and next service date. Office policy requires those details in the equipment-service log before the scale returns to use. The scale's log has not yet been updated.
questions.prompt: Which action completes the required office record?

choices.A: Enter only the next service date on the room calendar.
choices.B: File the technician's invoice with purchasing records without updating the log.
choices.C: Match the report to the scale, enter the required service details in its log, and retain the report under office policy.
choices.D: Copy the previous service entry and change only the date.

questions.explanation: The service report supplies the information required by the stated policy. Matching the serial number ensures that the entry belongs to the correct scale, and recording the actual service details supports future maintenance tracking. An invoice or calendar reminder alone does not complete this log.

questions.scenarioContext: For one completed visit, an explanation of benefits lists $80 in final patient responsibility. The ledger shows that the patient already paid $25 toward that same visit and that the payment was posted correctly. There are no other balances, pending claims, or adjustments. A draft patient statement still shows $80 due.
questions.prompt: How should the assistant reconcile the draft statement?

choices.A: Apply the posted $25 payment to the $80 responsibility and show $55 remaining due.
choices.B: Send the $80 statement because the explanation of benefits sets a new charge.
choices.C: Refund the $25 payment and mark the visit paid in full.
choices.D: Add the $25 payment to the $80 responsibility and show $105 due.

questions.explanation: The remaining balance is $80 - $25 = $55. An explanation of benefits describes claim processing and patient responsibility; it is not a separate bill and may not reflect payments already made to the office. The statement must account for the correctly posted payment.

questions.scenarioContext: During intake, a patient says, "I have several things to discuss, but at my last visit I only got through one." The medical assistant has not yet asked about the patient's concerns.
questions.prompt: Which response best helps establish the patient's agenda?

choices.A: "Let us finish the intake form, and then you can choose one concern."
choices.B: "Which concern do you think will take the provider the least time?"
choices.C: "What concerns would you like me to share with the provider today?"
choices.D: "Would you like me to list the concern from your last visit again?"

questions.explanation: An open-ended question invites the patient to identify their concerns before the team helps organize the visit. The assistant can record the concerns and relay them to the provider without deciding independently which concern deserves evaluation. Finishing a form before inviting the concerns can repeat the patient's experience of not being heard.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient who prefers to discuss health information in Spanish arrives with a 13-year-old child who offers to interpret. A qualified Spanish interpreter is available through the clinic's video service, and the patient agrees to use that service.
questions.prompt: Which action best supports an accurate intake conversation?

choices.A: Connect the qualified interpreter and address the patient directly.
choices.B: Ask the child to interpret and use the video service for unfamiliar words.
choices.C: Use a translation application and have the child confirm the responses.
choices.D: Ask questions in English more slowly and have the patient nod to confirm.

questions.explanation: A qualified interpreter supports accurate two-way communication, while the assistant continues speaking directly to the patient. Using a child as the primary interpreter can introduce errors and burden the child with sensitive information. Slower English or an unverified application does not meet this patient's stated communication need.

questions.scenarioContext: After identity verification, a caller reports lightheadedness beginning this morning after starting a new prescription yesterday. The caller says, "I have not fainted, but I want to know whether to take the next dose." The medical assistant has confirmed the medication name, the patient's callback number, and current location. Clinic policy requires immediate live transfer of symptom calls to the triage nurse, who is available.
questions.prompt: Which handoff best relays the call to the nurse?

choices.A: "The patient started a prescription yesterday and felt lightheaded this morning. I verified contact details and asked them to await your callback after appointments."
choices.B: "The patient started a prescription yesterday and felt lightheaded this morning. I advised skipping the next dose and will connect them for confirmation."
choices.C: "The patient has not fainted and wants prescription instructions. I verified contact details and will route a routine message about when to take the medicine."
choices.D: "The patient reports lightheadedness this morning after starting a prescription yesterday and asks about the next dose. I have verified details for live transfer."

questions.explanation: The handoff preserves the symptom, timing, patient question, and verified contact information while following the stated live-transfer policy. It avoids turning a reported sequence of events into a diagnosis or medication instruction. The absence of fainting does not justify minimizing or delaying the call.

questions.scenarioContext: At a noisy reception desk, a patient wearing hearing aids asks the medical assistant to repeat a simple check-in question. The patient says that facing the speaker and reducing background noise usually helps.
questions.prompt: Which adjustment best matches the patient's stated needs?

choices.A: Stay at the desk and repeat the question using a louder voice.
choices.B: Move to a quieter area and face the patient while speaking clearly.
choices.C: Write the question without first trying the patient's preferred approach.
choices.D: Stand beside the patient and speak slowly toward one hearing aid.

questions.explanation: The patient has identified effective adjustments for this brief conversation: less background noise and a clear view of the speaker. Speaking clearly while facing the patient supports those preferences. Raising the volume alone or substituting another method without considering the patient's preference may not improve understanding.

questions.scenarioContext: When greeted with an offered handshake, a patient steps back and says, "I prefer not to shake hands for personal reasons." The patient remains engaged in the conversation and is ready to check in.
questions.prompt: Which response best respects the patient's preference?

choices.A: "Would you tell me which belief prevents you from shaking hands?"
choices.B: "Thank you for letting me know. A verbal greeting is fine; how may I help?"
choices.C: "Should I tell the provider that physical contact is not acceptable today?"
choices.D: "Would you prefer that I greet your companion instead during this visit?"

questions.explanation: Acknowledging the preference and continuing with a verbal greeting allows the encounter to proceed respectfully. The patient does not need to justify a personal greeting preference. Declining a handshake does not establish that the patient refuses a clinical examination or wants communication redirected to a companion.

questions.scenarioContext: After a friendly visit, a patient asks a medical assistant to accept a request on the assistant's personal social media account so they can send future care questions there. Clinic policy directs patient communication through approved clinic channels and prohibits using personal accounts for patient care.
questions.prompt: Which reply best maintains a professional boundary?

choices.A: "I can accept the request if you only send questions about appointments."
choices.B: "I can answer general care questions there if you leave out your name."
choices.C: "You may follow my account, but please delete each message after I answer."
choices.D: "Please use the clinic portal or phone line for care questions; I keep my personal account separate."

questions.explanation: The response sets a clear boundary and offers appropriate ways to contact the clinic. It follows the stated policy without rejecting the patient's need for access. Limiting or deleting messages does not make a personal account an approved care channel.

questions.scenarioContext: A verified patient writes in the clinic portal, "Please have the provider change my work note from three days off to two weeks." The medical assistant can route requests but is not authorized to change the provider's work restrictions. No revised note has been approved.
questions.prompt: Which portal reply is most appropriate?

choices.A: "I will send your request to the provider for review. The clinic will contact you with the response."
choices.B: "I will prepare a two-week note today so you can give it to your employer."
choices.C: "Please tell your employer that the provider will extend the note after reviewing it."
choices.D: "Please bring a draft of the new note, and I will issue it with the provider's name."

questions.explanation: The reply clearly explains the next step without promising a decision that has not been made. Routing the request respects the assistant's stated role. Issuing a revised note or predicting approval would misrepresent the provider's decision.

questions.scenarioContext: An adult patient says, "I go by Alex and use they/them pronouns. Since my brain injury, I need extra time to answer." During intake, a companion repeatedly answers before Alex has time to speak. Alex says they want to answer the questions themselves.
questions.prompt: Which approach best supports Alex's participation?

choices.A: Ask the companion to give Alex's answers, then ask Alex to confirm them.
choices.B: Give Alex all the questions together so they can prepare several answers.
choices.C: Address Alex, ask one short question at a time, and allow time for a response.
choices.D: Repeat each question more loudly if Alex does not answer immediately.

questions.explanation: A direct conversation with one question at a time and adequate response time supports the need Alex described. A slower response does not establish that the companion should speak for Alex. Respectful communication also uses the name and pronouns the patient provided.

questions.scenarioContext: A medical assistant notices that a coworker has twice left the callback-number field blank on patient message forms. The omissions have required extra calls to obtain the numbers. No urgent message is currently waiting.
questions.prompt: Which statement provides the most constructive initial feedback?

choices.A: "Could we talk privately? Two messages lacked callback numbers, which delayed follow-up. Can we review the message checklist?"
choices.B: "Could you explain the missing numbers at the staff meeting so everyone can learn from them?"
choices.C: "Could you ask me to check each of your messages before sending it from now on?"
choices.D: "Could you be more careful with paperwork? The team needs everyone to improve."

questions.explanation: Private feedback that identifies specific observations, their effect, and a practical improvement supports teamwork. The message checklist gives both coworkers a concrete reference. A public discussion focused on one coworker or a vague request to be more careful is less useful for correcting this specific problem.

questions.scenarioContext: After speaking with the provider about an unexpected diagnosis, a patient becomes tearful while waiting for checkout instructions. The patient says, "I just need a moment." There is no immediate safety concern.
questions.prompt: Which response best combines supportive words and nonverbal behavior?

choices.A: Stand at the doorway and say, "Try to focus on the positive while I finish checkout."
choices.B: Continue typing and say, "I am listening; let me know when you are ready to leave."
choices.C: Hold the patient's hand without asking and say, "I know exactly how you feel."
choices.D: Pause the task, sit at a comfortable distance, and say, "Take your time; I am here."

questions.explanation: Pausing, allowing silence, and offering calm presence acknowledge the patient's expressed need. Sitting at a comfortable distance avoids assuming that touch would be welcome. Reassurance that redirects the patient toward positive thinking or continued typing can communicate that the patient should hurry past their distress.

questions.scenarioContext: During virtual-visit setup, a patient can see the medical assistant, but the audio repeatedly cuts out. The assistant misses several words when the patient describes the reason for the visit. Clinic policy permits approved connection troubleshooting and requires notifying the clinician if effective communication cannot be restored.
questions.prompt: Which action best addresses the communication problem?

choices.A: Continue intake and infer the missing words from the patient's visible expression.
choices.B: Record that the patient gave no additional concerns and complete the connection.
choices.C: Explain the audio problem, try the approved troubleshooting steps, and notify the clinician if it persists.
choices.D: End the video encounter and record it as completed because the patient successfully connected.

questions.explanation: The assistant should acknowledge an unreliable connection instead of treating partially heard information as complete. Approved troubleshooting may restore communication; persistent difficulty must be reported so the clinician can determine an appropriate next step. Connecting to a platform alone does not establish that a usable clinical exchange occurred.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient with low vision says they use a screen reader and would like to review a routine clinic information sheet independently. The clinic has an accessible electronic version tested for screen-reader use, as well as its usual small-print paper version.
questions.prompt: Which response best meets the patient's stated preference?

choices.A: "I can give the paper copy to your companion so they can read it later."
choices.B: "I can provide the accessible electronic version for your screen reader."
choices.C: "I can send a photograph of the paper sheet for your screen reader."
choices.D: "I can summarize the sheet aloud instead of providing your own copy."

questions.explanation: The accessible electronic version matches the patient's stated method of reading and supports independent review. A photograph of text may not provide usable text or reading order for a screen reader. Relying on a companion or an oral summary replaces the requested method despite an appropriate version being available.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient tells the medical assistant, "I have reported twice that staff call me by the wrong name, and it keeps happening." The patient is calm but asks to speak with someone who can address the repeated problem. Clinic policy allows documenting the preferred name in the designated field and referring unresolved service complaints to the office manager.
questions.prompt: Which response best addresses this complaint?

choices.A: "I am sorry this has continued. I will confirm the name you want us to use and ask the office manager to speak with you."
choices.B: "I will remind today's staff of your name; please let us know if it happens at another visit."
choices.C: "I understand your concern, but registration staff have many patients and may need more time."
choices.D: "I will change your name in my notes, and you can explain the problem again at checkout."

questions.explanation: The response acknowledges the repeated problem, confirms the patient's preference, and offers the policy-defined escalation the patient requested. The assistant should record the confirmed preference in the designated field and relay the complaint objectively. Another informal reminder alone does not address a complaint that remains unresolved after repeated reports.

questions.scenarioContext: At the front desk, a visitor says, "If you do not let me into the treatment area, I will hit you," and starts moving toward the staff-only doorway. Clinic policy directs staff to move to safety, warn nearby staff, and activate the designated emergency/security response for an immediate threat.
questions.prompt: Which action best follows the stated policy?

choices.A: Stand in the doorway and explain that the visitor must calm down before entering.
choices.B: Move to safety, alert nearby staff, and activate the emergency/security response.
choices.C: Invite the visitor into an empty examination room for a private conversation.
choices.D: Continue discussing the complaint while waiting to see whether the visitor enters.

questions.explanation: An explicit threat paired with movement toward a restricted area calls for the stated safety response. The assistant should create distance and summon help rather than try to resolve the complaint alone. Blocking the doorway or moving into a secluded room can increase exposure to the threatening visitor.

questions.scenarioContext: An older adult's daughter requests a copy of the patient's office records. She presents an advance directive naming her as health care agent only when specified conditions are met. The office has not verified whether her authority is currently effective. The patient is not present, and no other authorization or disclosure basis has been established. Clinic policy routes uncertain representative authority to the privacy officer for verification under applicable law.
questions.prompt: How should the medical assistant handle this request?

choices.A: Release the records after confirming that the daughter's name appears in the directive.
choices.B: Release the records after confirming that the daughter is listed as the emergency contact.
choices.C: Reject the request because an agent cannot exercise a patient's record-access rights.
choices.D: Refer the document for verification of the daughter's current authority before releasing records.

questions.explanation: A health care agent's authority and its effective conditions must be verified under applicable law before relying on that authority for this request. The document's existence does not establish that its activation conditions are satisfied, and emergency-contact status does not itself establish representative authority. An authorized personal representative may exercise applicable record-access rights within the scope of that authority.

questions.scenarioContext: An adult with decision-making capacity arrives for a routine blood draw. Before venipuncture, the patient withdraws their arm and says, "I do not want this test today." The order remains active, and no emergency exists. Clinic policy requires staff to document a refusal and inform the ordering provider.
questions.prompt: Which response appropriately respects the patient's decision?

choices.A: Explain that the active order requires completion of the blood draw today.
choices.B: Stop preparation, acknowledge the refusal, and document and report it according to policy.
choices.C: Ask the accompanying spouse to authorize the blood draw in the patient's place.
choices.D: Offer to collect a smaller sample and continue unless the patient objects again.

questions.explanation: A patient with decision-making capacity may refuse a recommended procedure, including after an order has been placed. The assistant should stop, document the refusal objectively, and notify the provider so questions or concerns can be addressed. Neither the active order nor the spouse's preference overrides this patient's refusal.

questions.scenarioContext: A medical assistant discovers a transposed blood pressure value in their authenticated electronic entry. The correct value is available on the original measurement record. A supervisor says, "Delete the old entry so the mistake will not show." Clinic policy requires corrections to preserve the original entry and identify the correction's author, date, time, and reason; the assistant is authorized to correct their own entries through this process.
questions.prompt: Which action best protects record integrity?

choices.A: Use the correction process to enter the verified value and preserve the original entry and audit trail.
choices.B: Delete the original entry and reenter the verified value using the original date and time.
choices.C: Leave the incorrect value unchanged and place the verified value in a private reminder file.
choices.D: Replace the value under the supervisor's login because the supervisor requested the change.

questions.explanation: The authorized correction process makes the record accurate while preserving the history of the change. Concealing an authenticated entry or using another person's login compromises accountability and violates the stated policy. A supervisor's instruction does not justify hiding an error; pressure to bypass the process should be escalated through the clinic's designated channel.

questions.scenarioContext: A cardiology office treating a referred patient requests the medication list and recent laboratory results needed for today's consultation. The medical assistant has verified the recipient, treatment purpose, and secure destination through the clinic's approved process. The clinic permits this provider-to-provider treatment disclosure without a separate patient authorization. No additional law restricts these records. A coworker suggests delaying the disclosure until a signed authorization is obtained and applying HIPAA's minimum-necessary standard to the disclosure.
questions.prompt: Which action correctly applies HIPAA to this request?

choices.A: Hold the records until the patient signs a separate disclosure authorization.
choices.B: Send only the medication names because minimum necessary bars sharing the laboratory results.
choices.C: Send the requested records securely under policy; this treatment disclosure is exempt from minimum necessary.
choices.D: Send a deidentified summary because identifiable records cannot be shared for a referral without authorization.

questions.explanation: HIPAA generally permits disclosures between health care providers for treatment without a separate patient authorization, and its minimum-necessary standard does not apply to these treatment disclosures or requests. The verified recipient, secure destination, stated policy, and absence of an additional legal restriction support sending these records. This exception does not grant unrelated staff unrestricted internal chart access.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient has signed the consent form for an office skin biopsy. Before the procedure begins, the patient asks the medical assistant, "Could this leave a scar, and are there other options? I signed because I thought I had to." The physician who will perform the procedure is available. Clinic policy assigns the procedure-specific discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives to that physician.
questions.prompt: What should the medical assistant do?

choices.A: Show the patient the signature and explain that the consent discussion is complete.
choices.B: Read the standard handout and proceed if the patient does not ask another question.
choices.C: Explain the biopsy's individual risks and select an alternative for the patient to consider.
choices.D: Pause preparation and ask the physician to address the questions and confirm the patient's voluntary decision.

questions.explanation: Informed consent involves understanding and a voluntary choice, not merely a signature. The physician must address this patient's procedure-specific questions and concerns about feeling pressured before proceeding. The assistant supports the process by pausing preparation and obtaining that discussion rather than substituting an independent risk-and-treatment explanation.

questions.scenarioContext: At a Florida pediatric office, an 8-year-old tells the medical assistant, "My dad hit me with his belt last night." The assistant sees linear bruises on the child's upper arm. The applicable Florida reporting rule requires a person who knows or has reasonable cause to suspect child abuse by a parent or caregiver to report immediately to the central abuse hotline. Clinic procedure also calls for notifying the provider and recording objective observations without delaying the required report.
questions.prompt: Which action fulfills the assistant's responsibility?

choices.A: Immediately report the suspicion to the hotline, notify the provider, and document observations and the child's statement.
choices.B: Notify the provider and wait for the provider to confirm abuse before contacting the hotline.
choices.C: Ask the father to explain the bruises and report only if he admits causing them.
choices.D: Schedule a follow-up examination and report if additional bruises appear at that visit.

questions.explanation: The child's statement and the observed bruises support reasonable suspicion under the reporting rule provided. The assistant must report immediately rather than investigate, obtain an admission, or wait for proof. Provider notification and objective documentation support care and accountability but do not replace or delay the required report.

questions.scenarioContext: A medical assistant notices a neighbor's name on the appointment schedule but has no assigned role in that visit. A coworker suggests opening the neighbor's chart to confirm a rumor about substance use and says patients with that history should receive less attention. Clinic policy permits record access only for assigned work and requires equitable care and reporting of suspected privacy or conduct violations.
questions.prompt: Which response best applies confidentiality and professional ethics?

choices.A: Open the chart to determine whether the rumor justifies changing the patient's care.
choices.B: Decline the chart access and address the inappropriate request and bias through the designated supervisor.
choices.C: Ask a staff member assigned to the visit to check the rumor and share only the diagnosis.
choices.D: Avoid opening the chart but recommend moving the patient's appointment to a less busy day.

questions.explanation: Curiosity and neighborhood familiarity do not create a work-related need to access protected information. The proposed access violates the stated privacy policy, and the suggestion to reduce attention based on a stigmatized history raises a separate ethical concern about equitable care. The assistant should use the designated reporting channel without opening the record or spreading the rumor.

questions.scenarioContext: A patient calls a primary care office with questions about home blood pressure readings and asks whether to take an extra antihypertensive tablet. The medical assistant can collect information and relay clinician instructions but is not authorized to select medication doses. There is no patient-specific dose-adjustment order or standing protocol. Clinic policy requires medication-adjustment questions to be routed promptly to a licensed clinician.
questions.prompt: Which action remains within the assistant's authorized role?

choices.A: Recommend an extra tablet if the reported reading is higher than the last office reading.
choices.B: Recommend withholding the next dose until the patient can attend a follow-up appointment.
choices.C: Record the readings, symptoms, and request, and route them promptly to the clinician without choosing a dose.
choices.D: Tell the patient to use a family member's dose-adjustment instructions until the clinician responds.

questions.explanation: Collecting information and promptly relaying the request are within the assistant's stated role. Selecting an extra dose or advising a medication hold would create a treatment decision without an authorized order or protocol. Another patient's instructions do not authorize a dose change for this patient.
